leaks.title: Three positions carry 33% of all losses
leaks.fix: Set a hard cash ceiling per position — ₹8,232, the size of one average win — and work quantity backwards from it so no single idea can do this again.

leaks.title: A 8-trade losing streak with no circuit breaker
leaks.evidence: The run cost −₹23,217 before it ended on its own.
leaks.fix: Cap the day at ₹16,463 of loss. Hitting it means the market isn't paying today and the terminal gets closed.

leaks.title: Overtrading on busy days
leaks.evidence: Days with 4–6 trades account for −₹10,221 across 5 trades at 0% wins.
leaks.fix: Give yourself a hard count of three trades a day. Scarcity forces you to wait for the setup instead of inventing one.

leaks.title: Short-term trades quietly becoming investments
leaks.evidence: 5 positions carried beyond the day, 0% profitable, −₹10,221 net.
leaks.fix: Name the holding period at entry and write it down. A trade that becomes a long-term hold after it moves against you is just an unexecuted stop.

traits.name: The disposition effect
traits.now: Losing trades are held 2.4 days on average; winners only 0.0.
traits.why: Selling a winner confirms you were right; selling a loser admits you were wrong. So winners get sold quickly to lock in the good feeling, and losers are kept in the hope of being proven right later.
traits.ideal: Holding time is driven by the plan and the price, never by whether the position is currently green or red.

traits.name: Moving the goalposts
traits.now: 6 positions lost more than half their value before being closed.
traits.why: A stop that exists only in your head is easy to move. Each time price reaches it, a new reason appears for giving the trade more room, and the planned small loss becomes a large one.
traits.ideal: Stops are placed with the broker at entry, so moving them requires a deliberate, visible action.

traits.name: Tilt
traits.now: Your longest losing run was 8 trades in a row, costing ₹23,217.
traits.why: After several losses, frustration takes over decision-making. Each new loss lowers the bar for the next entry, until trading becomes a way to vent rather than a process.
traits.ideal: A daily loss limit and a maximum number of consecutive losses, after which trading stops for the day.

traits.name: Martingale instinct
traits.now: After a loss, your next position is 40% bigger than after a win.
traits.why: Doubling up feels like a way to recover faster. It is the oldest gambling instinct: increase the bet to win back what was lost. It concentrates risk exactly when your judgement is weakest.
traits.ideal: Size is fixed by a rule (for example, a percentage of capital) and never increases after a loss.

traits.name: Chasing the same name
traits.now: 3 times you re-entered the same name on the same day you lost on it, losing ₹4,318 more.
traits.why: Losing on a specific stock or contract makes it personal. Re-entering is an attempt to win back from that particular instrument, as if it owed you something.
traits.ideal: After a loss on a name, that name is off-limits for the rest of the day.

traits.name: Weekday blind spot
traits.now: Thursday is your worst day: 10 trades, 40% win rate, −₹20,968.
traits.why: Patterns tied to a day of the week are often about you, not the market: energy levels, routines, expiries, or what happened the day before.
traits.ideal: Days that consistently lose get smaller size or no trading until the reason is understood.

traits.name: Holding through events
traits.now: Trades held overnight lost ₹10,221, while same-day trades made ₹1.66L.
traits.why: Overnight positions face news and gaps you cannot react to. If your edge is intraday, holding overnight swaps a skill-based game for a coin flip.
traits.ideal: Overnight risk is taken only by design, sized for a gap against you.

traits.name: Rule erosion
traits.now: Your later trades won less often (42%) than your earlier ones (56%).
traits.why: Rules are easiest to follow at the start. Each small exception that works out makes the next one easier, until the rules are mostly gone.
traits.ideal: Rules are written, checked before each trade, and reviewed weekly.

more.name: Boredom trades
more.now: Days with a single trade made ₹3,503; busy days lost ₹10,221.
more.why: Your first trade of the day is usually your best one, chosen with patience. Extra trades come from restlessness, not opportunity.
more.ideal: After the planned trade, the platform closes unless a pre-defined second setup appears.

more.name: Short-term thinking in long trades
more.now: Positions you carried for days lost ₹10,221, while your quick trades did better.
more.why: A trade that was meant to be quick becomes a "long-term investment" once it goes red. The story changes to justify not closing it.
more.ideal: The holding period is set at entry. A short-term trade that fails is closed, not reclassified.

more.name: Late-session fatigue
more.now: Your late-session trades return much less on average than your early ones.
more.why: Decision quality drops as the session goes on. Attention fades and the bar for a good setup quietly lowers.
more.ideal: The most important decisions are made when you are freshest; late trading is limited or stopped.

more.name: Calendar fixation
more.now: Your best weekday (Monday) and worst (Thursday) differ by ₹93,804.
more.why: Large differences between days point to routine and mindset rather than market structure. Your best day shows how you trade when conditions suit you.
more.ideal: Recreate the conditions of your best day (preparation, timing, mood) on the others.

more.name: Perfectionism after loss
more.now: Your win rate after a loss (41%) is well below your rate after a win (56%).
more.why: A loss can trigger an urge to make the next trade perfect, leading to over-analysis, hesitation, then a forced entry when the move has already happened.
more.ideal: The trade after a loss uses the exact same checklist. No extra conditions, no shortcuts.

more.name: Self-attribution after streaks
more.now: You had a 5-trade winning streak and a 8-trade losing streak.
more.why: Winning streaks feel like skill and losing streaks feel like bad luck. Both are often the same process meeting different market conditions.
more.ideal: Size and rules stay the same through streaks of either kind.

net.ideal: Net P&L after costs is the only number that pays. Judge every change to your trading by its effect here.

gross.ideal: Gross P&L should comfortably exceed costs; if it barely does, trade less, not more.

costs.now: Costs were 0% of what your winners made.
costs.ideal: Costs under 15–20% of gross profit. Fewer trades with larger targets get you there.

winrate.ideal: Win rate only matters alongside payoff. 40% with 2:1 winners beats 60% with 1:2.

payoff.now: Average win is 2.52× the average loss.
payoff.ideal: A payoff above 1.5 gives room for a normal win rate to be profitable.

avgwin.ideal: Winners run to a planned target instead of being taken at the first sign of profit.

avgloss.ideal: Losers closed at a pre-set stop, so the average loss is smaller than the average win.

pf.ideal: A profit factor above 1.3 after costs is a sustainable edge.

worst.now: Your worst trade was ₹14,537, about 1.8 average wins.
worst.ideal: The worst trade is no bigger than one or two average wins.

leaks.now: Losses are spread across many trades.
